one_line: A debunk of the "Qwen 3.8 27B 2x faster on Mac" headline: the 2x comes from speculative decoding with a 1.2 GB draft model, not the Splash engine, and the built-in multi-token-prediction head gives smaller gains for free. Measure effective tokens/s with warm and cold cache, not decode speed.
summary: The host examines Inco AI's Splash, an Apple Silicon inference engine that runs only Qwen 3.8 27B and 35B, and its headline numbers of 144 tok/s on an M5 Max and 74 tok/s on an M5 Pro. He explains that decode on Apple Silicon is memory-bandwidth bound, so 74 tok/s is about 3.6x the bandwidth ceiling for a 15 GB 4-bit model, which points to speculative decoding as the real source of the speedup. The 2x headline compares Splash (with a draft model) against OMLX, which had no draft support for Qwen at the time, and Inco's own methodology notes say the benchmark does not isolate the engine. Qwen 3.8 27B reportedly ships with a multi-token-prediction head that can act as a draft model without any download, giving about 23 to 30 percent gains in community tests, largest on code and JSON and smallest on chat. The more useful finding is that decode tok/s hides prefill time: a 32k-token prompt takes 96 s to first token cold but 282 ms warm, and effective tok/s moves from 8.9 to 53. Splash has real advantages for long multi-turn agent sessions and concurrency, but it needs an M3 or newer, macOS 26.4, at least 36 GB of memory and a proprietary 17.4 GB package. The suggested action is to run one prompt cold and warm, time the full response, and compare.
speakers: Host (Kai Explains channel, unnamed in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: The 144 and 74 tok/s headlines are not explained by the engine alone. Decode on a Mac is memory-bandwidth bound, since the full 15 GB of 4-bit weights must cross the memory bus for every token.
key_ideas.detail: An M5 Pro at 307 GB/s with a 15.1 GB model has a ceiling of about 20 tok/s. Splash reports 74 tok/s, about 3.6x that ceiling, which the speaker says no kernel can deliver. The extra throughput has to come from generating several tokens per weight pass.

key_ideas.idea: Speculative decoding explains the speed. A small draft model proposes about 7 tokens per step, and the large model verifies them in one pass.
key_ideas.detail: Splash's draft model, D-Flash 2 (1.2 GB), gets roughly 3 to 4 of about 7 proposals accepted on average. Accepted tokens cost one memory pass together, and rejected ones are discarded. The draft model does the guessing and the big model does the approving.

key_ideas.idea: The 2x headline is speculative decoding against no speculative decoding, not Splash against OMLX. Inco's own methodology notes say the benchmark does not isolate the engine.
key_ideas.detail: OMLX had an open feature request for Qwen draft support and had none at benchmark time, while it did support drafting for Gemma. Splash ran 74 tok/s and OMLX 38 tok/s. The speaker says the vendor disclosed this in its blog post and downstream coverage dropped it.

key_ideas.idea: Qwen 3.8 27B ships with a built-in multi-token-prediction head that can serve as a draft model, so speculative gains may be available without Splash or new hardware.
key_ideas.detail: Community reports cited: a 3090 went from 31 to 41 tok/s (~30%), a laptop 5090 from 37 to 51, and a Mac on llama.cpp gained about 23%. These are speaker-cited figures I did not verify. The gain depends on workload: code, JSON and tool calls accept more drafts than open chat.

key_ideas.idea: Inco's 2x was measured on the most draft-friendly workload available, SpeedBench coding with reasoning on, timing decode of reasoning tokens. Chat gains would be smaller.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker argues that a setup with drafting against one without it will look like 2x on repetitive code, and that this result should not be generalised to normal use.

key_ideas.idea: Decode tok/s is the wrong metric for agent workflows. Prefill (time to first token) dominates long prompts, so the number that matters is effective tok/s across the whole response.
key_ideas.detail: On a 32k-token prompt with a cold cache, Splash takes 96 s to first token and OMLX 317 s. Decode of 1024 tokens takes about 19 s. In one developer's M1 Max test with 8.5k context, the interface showed 57 tok/s, but effective throughput was about 3 tok/s because prefill was about 94% of the response time.

key_ideas.idea: Prompt caching changes the experience more than the draft model does. Warm-cache prefill drops from 96 s to 282 ms, and effective tok/s goes from 8.9 to 53 on the same prompt.
key_ideas.detail: In long multi-turn agent sessions, the speaker reports first-token latency of 2049 ms for OMLX against 282 ms for Splash, about 7x. Splash also handled 16 concurrent 32k-token requests on a 48 GB machine where a general memory policy handled 9.

key_ideas.idea: Splash's specialization is narrow: two models, compiled kernels and fixed-layout weights, and a memory planner that refuses to boot with a memory report when the model will not fit. The hardware requirements are tight.
key_ideas.detail: It requires an M3 or newer, macOS 26.4 and at least 36 GB of unified memory (48 GB recommended). The model comes as a proprietary 17.4 GB package, so existing MLX and GGUF files cannot be used. It exposes OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs, which the speaker says let Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode connect with one config line.

techniques.name: Measure effective tokens per second, cold and warm
techniques.how: Send one real prompt with a large context (about 32k tokens in the video) to a cold cache, then send it again warm. Time the full response from send to last token with a stopwatch or script. Compute effective tok/s as output tokens divided by total wall time, and report time to first token separately. Do not use the decode rate shown in the UI.
techniques.when: Before choosing a local model or runtime for coding agents or long multi-turn sessions, and before publishing any local-inference benchmark.

techniques.name: Enable the model's built-in multi-token-prediction head as a draft
techniques.how: On Qwen 3.8 27B, enable multi-token prediction in the runtime you use, then set draft depth to 2 or 3. The speaker does not show exact flags or config keys, so check the runtime's docs. Compare decode and effective tok/s with it on and off, using the same prompt and settings.
techniques.when: When running Qwen 3.8 27B locally and you want a speedup without changing hardware or downloading a new model. Expect bigger gains on code, JSON and tool-call output and smaller gains on chat.

techniques.name: Bandwidth ceiling sanity check
techniques.how: Divide memory bandwidth (GB/s) by the model's weight size in GB at its quantization. This gives the rough single-stream decode ceiling. For Qwen 3.8 27B at 4-bit, about 15.1 GB, on a 307 GB/s chip, that is about 20 tok/s. Reported speeds well above that imply speculative decoding or batching.
techniques.when: When reading a vendor benchmark, to check whether a headline tok/s number is physically plausible on the stated hardware.

techniques.name: Isolate the variable in a benchmark
techniques.how: Run the baseline and the candidate with the same model, quantization, draft settings, prompt, cache state and output length. Check whether the comparison includes speculative decoding on one side only, as in the Splash versus OMLX case. Publish the settings alongside the numbers.
techniques.when: When comparing inference engines or configurations, to make sure the speedup comes from the engine and not from a feature one side has and the other lacks.

techniques.name: Fail fast on memory
techniques.how: Before loading weights, compute the model plus KV cache requirement and compare it with available memory. Print a report and refuse to start when it will not fit, instead of crashing partway through a generation. The speaker presents this as a design choice in Splash.
techniques.when: When building a local serving layer on machines with fixed unified memory, so that long generations do not die late.

techniques.name: Point coding agents at a local OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible endpoint
techniques.how: The speaker says Splash exposes OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs, so Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode can be pointed at it with one config line. The exact key or base URL is not shown in the video.
techniques.when: When you want to run an agent harness against a local model. Verify tool-call and streaming behaviour yourself, as the speaker did not test it in the video.

tools: Splash (Inco AI inference engine for Apple Silicon, Apache 2.0, Qwen 3.8 27B and 35B only)
LM Studio (shipped Splash as a selectable backend)

numbers.claim: Splash on an M5 Max MacBook Pro: 144 tok/s (memory bandwidth 614 GB/s)
Splash on a 48 GB M5 Pro: 74 tok/s, against OMLX at 38 tok/s, which is the 2x headline
M5 Pro bandwidth 307 GB/s, 15.1 GB 4-bit model, theoretical decode ceiling about 20 tok/s; 74 tok/s is about 3.6x that
Draft model D-Flash 2 is 1.2 GB, proposes about 7 tokens per step, and about 3 to 4 are accepted on average
32k-token prompt, cold cache: time to first token 96 s for Splash, 317 s for OMLX
Decode of 1024 tokens at 54 tok/s is about 19 s, so the output is much shorter than the prefill wait
Developer's M1 Max case: 57 tok/s shown in the UI at 8.5k context, about 3 tok/s effective, with prefill about 94% of response time
Same 32k prompt, warm cache: time to first token 282 ms (from 96 s cold); effective tok/s 53 warm against 8.9 cold
Long agent sessions: first-token latency 2049 ms for OMLX against 282 ms for Splash, about 7x
Concurrency: 16 simultaneous 32k-token requests on a 48 GB machine for Splash, against 9 for a general-purpose memory policy
Community multi-token-prediction gains (speaker-cited): 3090 31 to 41 tok/s (about 30%); laptop 5090 37 to 51 tok/s; a Mac on llama.cpp about 23%
Splash requirements: M3 or newer, macOS 26.4, at least 36 GB unified memory (48 GB recommended); 17.4 GB proprietary package

hot_takes: The 2x headline is a speculative-decoding-versus-none comparison presented as an engine win. The vendor's own methodology notes disclose this, and coverage dropped the caveat.
Decode tokens per second is a misleading metric for agent work. Prefill and prompt caching matter more to the experience, and the cache win (6x) is bigger than the draft win (2x).
Qwen 3.8 27B's built-in multi-token-prediction head may give most of the speedup for free, with no new runtime or hardware.
Splash's narrow support (two models, M3 or newer, 36 GB or more, proprietary format) makes it useful only for a minority of Mac owners, despite the broad headline.

relevance.why: InferCraft (L2B) already plans speculative decoding (EAGLE-3) and KV-cache strategies, and L4 observability covers latency. This video's point that decode tok/s hides prefill and that baselines must match the feature set applies directly to InferCraft benchmarks.
relevance.action: Add cold and warm time-to-first-token and effective tok/s (end-to-end output tokens divided by wall time) to InferCraft benchmark reports, and require each comparison to list whether speculative decoding is on for both sides before publishing a speedup.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps the Claude Code CLI. The video's claim that Claude Code can be pointed at a local Anthropic-compatible endpoint is relevant only if ProsHarness ever runs cheap or local subagents. The claim is unverified.
relevance.action: If ProsHarness ever routes subagent runs to a local model, test a local Anthropic-compatible endpoint on a long multi-turn run and measure warm-cache effective tok/s before relying on it.
